quote: > One encounter, two failures: a COWS-threshold buprenorphine start precipitated withdrawal in a fentanyl-exposed patient, and the recovery is methadone or low-dose initiation - with acute pain treated alongside the MOUD, never instead of it.
problem: The TL;DR (repeated verbatim as the 'Shelf-level takeaway' exam card) describes a different case. In the MS3 page, naloxone precipitated the withdrawal, no buprenorphine was given, and acute pain is never managed. The page's own answer is to start buprenorphine in the ED now, not methadone or low-dose initiation.
whyItMatters: A learner who reads only the card takes away the wrong mechanism for this patient's withdrawal and the wrong next step (avoid a standard buprenorphine start). The page teaches the opposite. As a free-standing claim, 'the recovery is methadone or low-dose initiation' also leaves out that buprenorphine-precipitated withdrawal is usually treated first with more buprenorphine plus adjuncts.
evidence: Page text Q1/Q2 (naloxone-precipitated withdrawal) and Q5 'In this case... Buprenorphine is the practical answer — start it here'; Englander et al., JAMA Intern Med 2024 (ref 3), on managing precipitated withdrawal.
correction: > Two toxidromes, one encounter: naloxone reversed the overdose and precipitated withdrawal. Observe for re-sedation, treat the withdrawal, start buprenorphine in the building, and send him out with naloxone and a named follow-up.
verified: Read the whole page against the overlay; recall for precipitated-withdrawal management

quote: a shorter interval since the last drink at presentation
problem: The direction is reversed. In the cohort usually cited for this risk factor, patients who developed DT had gone MORE days since their last drink. Neither PAWSS nor the major reviews lists a short interval as a predictor of complicated withdrawal.
whyItMatters: A learner would treat someone who presents 2-3 days after the last drink (already inside the DT window) as lower risk, which is exactly the patient who goes on to DT.
evidence: Ferguson JA et al. Risk factors for delirium tremens development. J Gen Intern Med 1996;11:410-4 (PMID 8842933): on multivariable analysis, more days since last drink (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.09-1.61) and concurrent acute illness (OR 5.1) predicted DT.
correction: a longer interval since the last drink at presentation (already late in the withdrawal timeline)
verified: PubMed abstract PMID 8842933 retrieved via E-utilities

quote: (7–14 days from most SSRIs; 5–6 weeks from fluoxetine)
problem: The 7-day minimum washout before an MAOI comes from UK NHS SPS guidance. It is shorter than US FDA labeling, which requires at least 14 days after stopping sertraline, escitalopram, citalopram, paroxetine or fluvoxamine (at least 5 weeks after fluoxetine).
whyItMatters: A US learner or resident (the page also ships to residents) could start an MAOI 7 days after an SSRI, contrary to the label, with a risk of serotonin toxicity.
evidence: NHS SPS 'SSRIs to other antidepressants: switching in adults' (checked 2026-09-24): 'wait 7 to 14 days'. US prescribing information for sertraline, escitalopram, citalopram and paroxetine (Contraindications / Drug Interactions: at least 14 days); fluoxetine PI: at least 5 weeks.
correction: (at least 14 days from most SSRIs per US labeling — UK guidance allows 7–14; at least 5 weeks from fluoxetine)
verified: WebFetch of the cited SPS page; US labels from recall

quote: so this is not yet an adequate trial and not yet a failed one
problem: This mixes up how much the patient improved with whether the trial was adequate. On the page's own definition (adequate dose for ≥6-8 weeks), and with the stem stating she is 'on an adequately dosed SSRI' at 6 weeks, she is already at the lower bound of an adequate trial. A minimal response does not make the trial inadequate.
whyItMatters: Learners come away thinking a small response resets the trial clock. That contradicts the dose × duration rule the page teaches and can prolong an ineffective trial.
evidence: Page's own Q3 definition ('adequate dose for adequate duration (≥6–8 weeks)'); CANMAT 2023 MDD update (dose optimisation or switch when improvement is <20-25% after an adequate early trial).
correction: so it is not a partial response — and although at 6 weeks on an adequate dose she has reached the lower bound of an adequate trial, it is not yet clearly a failed one

quote: a syndrome defined by ≥2 weeks of depressed mood and/or anhedonia (loss of pleasure) plus associated neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms, causing functional impairment
problem: The definition leaves out the core DSM-5-TR count: at least 5 of 9 symptoms present during the same 2-week period, at least one of which is depressed mood or anhedonia.
whyItMatters: The symptom count separates MDD from adjustment disorder, subthreshold depression and other specified depressive disorder. The page's own differential ('does not meet full MDD criteria') depends on it, and the shelf tests it.
evidence: DSM-5-TR (2022), Major Depressive Disorder Criterion A.
correction: a syndrome defined by ≥5 of 9 symptoms over the same ≥2-week period — at least one being depressed mood or anhedonia (loss of pleasure), the rest neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms — causing clinically significant distress or impairment

quote: depressive symptoms ≥2 years at lower intensity
problem: 'Lower intensity' is the DSM-IV concept of dysthymia. DSM-5-TR persistent depressive disorder combines chronic MDD and dysthymia, and full MDD criteria may be met throughout the 2 years.
whyItMatters: Learners may wrongly rule out PDD in a patient with chronic, full-severity depression.
evidence: DSM-5-TR (2022), Persistent Depressive Disorder, Criteria A-B and specifiers (with persistent major depressive episode).
correction: depressed mood most days for ≥2 years (severity may reach full MDD criteria)

quote: augment with an atypical antipsychotic (e.g., aripiprazole), lithium, or T3; consider psychiatry referral
problem: The TRD step leaves out esketamine nasal spray, which is FDA-approved for TRD (adjunct since 2019, monotherapy since January 2025, under a REMS). It also names only aripiprazole among FDA-approved adjunctive antipsychotics; brexpiprazole, cariprazine and quetiapine XR are also approved.
whyItMatters: A national MS3 audience sits a shelf that can test esketamine as a TRD option. The ladder as written implies the TRD options stop at augmentation and ECT.
evidence: Spravato (esketamine) US prescribing information, TRD indication (monotherapy approval Jan 2025); Rexulti, Vraylar (2022) and Seroquel XR adjunctive MDD labels.
correction: augment with an atypical antipsychotic (e.g., aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine, quetiapine XR), lithium, or T3; know that esketamine nasal spray is FDA-approved for TRD (REMS, certified setting); consider psychiatry referral

quote: When in doubt about safety, arrange same-day evaluation, and bring your supervising resident or attending in before any disposition is settled.
problem: Q7 has the learner assess ideation, intent, plan and means and build a safety plan, which is real risk work under the library's own scope rule. The page carries no crisis block, unlike the suicide COTW.
whyItMatters: A learner building a safety plan here has no crisis contacts to put in it. The 2026-09-01 review flagged the same gap (MS3V10-F010, quote since reworded), and it has not been fixed.
evidence: Standing editorial policy 2 (crisis block required where the learner is doing risk work); prior finding MS3V10-F010.
correction:
When in doubt about safety, arrange same-day evaluation, and bring your supervising resident or attending in before any disposition is settled.
